query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In lightweight, Mg-containing high-entropy alloys, thermal exposure induces diffusion-driven segregation of Mg from a metastable solid solution to form Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that serve as nucleation sites for the development of a continuous, protective mixed oxide scale (involving MgO and other oxides such as Al2O3). This microstructural evolution decelerates oxidation kinetics and improves corrosion resistance relative to the initial as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, metastable single‐phase lightweight high‐entropy alloy (density below 6 g/cm³) with Mg in solid solution along with other constituents (e.g., Al, Cu, Zn, Gd).
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging (or heat treatment) at elevated temperatures that trigger phase transformation and Mg diffusion.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation tests in air and corrosion tests under a corrosive environment (e.g., cyclic saline exposure), performed under conditions where diffusion is active but excessive coarsening is avoided.
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitated Mg-rich intermetallic compounds forming along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Upon thermal exposure, Mg diffuses out of the metastable matrix and segregates to form fine intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates act as catalysts for the nucleation and growth of a protective mixed oxide layer (including MgO and potentially Al2O3), which retards oxygen ingress and limits subsequent corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial as-cast state, the thermally aged alloy will exhibit a lower mass gain during oxidation (indicative of slower oxidation kinetics) and a reduced corrosion rate (e.g., lower current densities in electrochemical tests) as a direct result of the formation of a dense, adherent oxide scale guided by Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, non-equilibrium single-phase alloy without significant intermetallic precipitation or oxide scale development.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid for alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ that contain a modest Mg content sufficient to generate distinct Mg-rich intermetallics upon aging, and under exposure conditions where thermal activation of diffusion occurs (but not so high as to induce excessive coarsening or melting).
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of Mg segregation, the composition and continuity of the mixed oxide, and the quantitative improvement in oxidation and corrosion resistance are uncertain and likely depend on the exact alloy composition, Mg level, and aging temperature/time parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy. One set remains in the as-cast, metastable state while the other set undergoes a controlled thermal aging treatment designed to promote phase separation. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation and corrosive conditions. Use microstructural characterization (TEM, SEM, XRD) to assess the presence of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates and protective oxide scale formation, and measure oxidation kinetics (mass gain over time) and corrosion performance (electrochemical tests).
measurements: Oxide scale composition and continuity (via XPS and SEM/EDS)
Identification and quantification of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates (TEM/XRD)
Corrosion current density and pitting density from electrochemical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation rate and improved corrosion resistance relative to the as-cast specimens, or if no distinct Mg-rich intermetallic phases and associated protective oxide scale are observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How does the combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering affect the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of an equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy, particularly regarding the formation of secondary phases due to interstitial elements?. System: Equiatomic NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (Nb: 16.67 at%, Mo: 16.67 at%, Ta: 16.67 at%, W: 16.67 at%, V: 16.67 at%, Ti: 16.67 at%) with oxygen introduction. Processing: Mechanical alloying of elemental powders (≥99.9% purity) in a high energy planetary ball mill with stainless steel balls/vial at a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 13:1 under high purity argon for 40 h; followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of the 40 h milled powders in a graphite die at 1400 °C for 10 min under 30 MPa pressure, with a heating rate of 100 °C/min and cooling to 500 °C at 300 °C/min. Question: What are the long-term oxidation mechanisms and kinetics of a novel refractory high entropy alloy (NV1) at 1000 °C and 1100 °C over an unprecedented duration of 200 hours, and how does the formation of a CrTaO4-based oxide influence its resistance compared to existing literature?. System: NV1 alloy (Al17.6Si2.9Ti5.4Cr25.2Nb15.2Mo20.3Ta13.4 at%); as-cast microstructure contains Mo-rich BCC dendrites, Cr-rich hexagonal phase, and Al-rich tetragonal phase.. Processing: Cold crucible levitation melting of high purity elemental raw materials (>99.9 wt%) to cast a 1.1 kg cone-shaped ingot; samples machined by electrical discharge machining and ground to 1200 grit; isothermal oxidation conducted in flowing dry air using a thermogravimetric analyser (SETARAM TAG 24-18S) and muffle furnace.. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours in flowing dry air; microstructural characterization performed at intervals of 1, 12, 40, 50, 100, and 200 hours..
